newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lufthansa, union talk as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lufthansa, union talk as strike looms.

text.p: German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG resumed talks on Monday aimed at reaching a wages deal by mid-week as a major union threatened to stage another round of work stoppages starting on Thursday.

Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber said in a magazine interview on Monday that he was hopeful of a breakthrough in talks with the DAG union, which represents pilots, flight attendants and many white-collar workers at the airline.
"I am still hopeful of reason and responsibility among the DAG leadership and that we will see a breakthrough in this round of talks," Weber told Germany's Focus magazine.

But DAG union chief Roland Issen said at the weekend that a lack of progress in the talks prompted the union, which represents many of the 50,000 workers at Lufthansa along with the OeTV public workers' union, to recommend that workers prepare for industrial action later this week.

The DAG on Monday again demanded that Lufthansa shorten the duration of its current pay offer from 27 months, which it said would allow the airline time to move jobs out of Germany and into new subsidiaries outside the union's control.
"Lufthansa management is required to make an offer with a shorter time period and a better offer more consistent with industry standards," top DAG negotiator Michael Tarp said.
Issen said Germany's main airport in Frankfurt would be hardest hit if there were a walkout but that flights from the major cities of Hamburg and Munich could also suffer.
The DAG last called work stoppages for two hours on November 11, forcing Lufthansa to ground about 35 of its flights and costing the airline an estimated 12 million marks ($7.7 million).

Lufthansa has already reached a pay deal with the OeTV union, which the DAG has rejected. Weber said the airline was committed to getting the DAG to accept the same contract, saying any changes would hurt the airline's union relations.

The two-year OeTV deal was reached in October and calls for workers to receive a one-off payment equal to one-third of a month's base pay. In addition, the airline said workers would receive a 1.7 percent pay rise in 1998.
The offer also included a one-off payment of either 500 marks in cash or 625 marks in Lufthansa stock as part of a unique profit-sharing scheme for a company that is still paritially state-owned.

The labour standoff comes at a critical time for the Frankfurt-based airline, which said in October that it was trying to rein in costs by as much as 20 percent to meet growing competition in the airline industry.

Weber said in the Focus interview that the April 1997 date under which European air space will be open to full competition threatens the ability of Lufthansa to compete because of the relatively high wages in Germany.
An airline official said pilots at Lufthansa can earn base salaries ranging from 65,000 to 247,000 marks, while flight attendants earn from 31,000 to 83,000 marks.

"We are prepared to reduce the costs in our core businesses," Weber said. "We have made concrete decisions to cut costs per flight kilometer by 20 percent in the next five years. That will save us 1.5 billion marks a year."

At the same time, he declined to explain how Lufthansa would seek to improve its service at a time when it has come under criticism in Germany about cost-cutting measures and while its high ticket prices compared to competitors are turning away potential passengers.
Lufthansa lost some 250,000 clients and some 50 million marks in sales to discount ticket offers in Germany from rival European airlines in the first half of 1996.

Weber said in particular that British-based airlines with cheaper cost structures would create "a difficult life" for Lufthansa after European skies are liberalised but said the airline was seeking to strengthen its international alliances. ($1=1.5522 Mark)
